Tear It Down or Fix It Up? When Redevelopment Makes Financial Sense

That tired house on a promising Tucson lot might be a renovation opportunity—or it might be a land play.

By Reddy Appraisal LLCOctober 22, 20262 min read

IN THIS ARTICLE

Compare renovation with redevelopmentGround the options in feasibilityConfirm what the parcel can supportMore in Land & Redevelopment ↗← All 24 articles

THE SHORT ANSWER

Southern Arizona has pockets where infill and renovation are attracting attention, but every parcel is different. Confirm development possibilities with the appropriate local planning authority before spending money on plans.

Compare renovation with redevelopment

That tired house on a promising Tucson lot might be a renovation opportunity—or it might be a land play. Before swinging a hammer, owners should compare the cost of repairing the existing structure with the potential value of a different legally permissible use. The most expensive option isn't necessarily the most profitable, and the cheapest fix isn't always the best long-term decision.

Ground the options in feasibility

Begin with the basics: zoning, lot dimensions, access, utilities, permitting, demolition costs, and construction estimates. Then look at recent sales of renovated homes, properties in similar condition, and vacant or redevelopment-oriented lots. Appraisers call the analysis of a property's reasonably probable, legally permissible, physically possible, and financially feasible use its highest and best use. That framework can help keep big redevelopment ideas grounded in market reality.

Confirm what the parcel can support

Southern Arizona has pockets where infill and renovation are attracting attention, but every parcel is different. Confirm development possibilities with the appropriate local planning authority before spending money on plans. For residential properties and land, Reddy Appraisal LLC can help owners understand current market value as one piece of a larger feasibility decision.
